newsitem.title: USA: Merger fireworks color US oil refiners' meeting.
newsitem.headline: Merger fireworks color US oil refiners' meeting.

text.p: With the largest merger in U.S. oil refining history inked this week, the talk of consolidation heard in many of the speeches at the annual National Petroleum Refiners Association (NPRA) meeting this week had a certain immediacy.

The 3,000 refining executives attending the 95th annual meeting of the NPRA were kept on their toes with blunt talk that profits would not be getting much better, and that strategic alliances were all the rage.

The mega-deal this week was Texaco Inc and Shell Oil Co's $10 billion merger of most of their U.S. downstream, with another chunk expected when state-owned Saudi Aramco agrees terms for merger of the Star Enterprises joint venture with Texaco.

Valero Energy Corp's purchase of Salomon Inc's Basis Refining unit for $485 million kicked off the week. Those two deals, like the host of consolidating deals last year, won praise from Wall Street, leaving many NPRA attendees perhaps with an "urge to merge."

"I think you'll see more and more consolidation and it'll come to a point where you can't do any more," Baines Manning, Valero Energy Corp's senior refining executive told Reuters in an interview Tuesday.
Executives said the message from the consolidations and the speeches were clear: Waiting for change could be fatal.

"Don't count on industry solutions. Don't wait for margins to get better, don't wait for Godot (who never arrives)," Daniel Yergin, president of Boston-based consultancy Cambridge Energy Research Associates told executives.
They were also told that the merging phase in the oil refining business will likely last for a long time.
"The consolidation time can last for decades and will likely come in waves," said Calvin Cobb managing director of Houston-based consultancy Ernst Young/Wright Killen.
Cobb and others also said those companies who will succeed are likely to be those with aggressive expansion plans.
"These high performers have decided that even in a mature industry they have and will continue to find a niche or other well-defined strategic position that will create shareholder value," Cobb said.
Another thread running through the meeting was the threat to refiner profitability a new proposal to toughen U.S. air quality standards would have.

"Of all the business entities facing impacts from new air quality standards, the petroleum refining industry is among the most exposed," said Thomas Wylie, Sun Co Inc's vice president of government relations.

The Environmental Protection Agency proposal, made public last year, would toughen the threshold for acceptable levels of smog and would also target much smaller dust particles than ever before but would not be felt until after the year 2000.
Wylie said that while estimates of total costs to U.S. refiners and other industry are still being evaluated, they are likely to soar into the hundreds of billions of dollars.
